title: The disease of arrogance
hook: no one with an atom's weight of arrogance enters the garden, and arrogance is rejecting truth and looking down on people (Muslim)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the heart as a lump of flesh, and your line: if the heart is sound. When your hand rested on your chest, what was going on in there? Today the diseases of that heart begin, one at a time. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-two.

A gathering in Medina. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says that no one with an atom's weight of arrogance in his heart will enter the garden. And a man in the room has a worry, and says it out loud. A man likes his clothes to be good, he says, and his sandals to be good. Is that it? Is a nice pair of sandals the thing that keeps a person out? It's an honest question, and the answer, recorded in Sahih Muslim, is a definition clear enough to fit on a sticky note. Today's word is what he was asking about: kibr, arrogance.

The answer comes in two halves. The first half: Allah is beautiful and loves beauty. So the sandals are fine. Caring how you look, owning something well made, isn't what the hadith means. The second half is the definition. Kibr is rejecting the truth and looking down on people. Two motions of the heart. Rejecting the truth: hearing something right and pushing it away, because of who said it, or because agreeing would cost face. Looking down on people: treating someone as smaller than you. Notice what isn't on the list. Money isn't. Looks aren't. Talent isn't. Next, a picture of it from the Qur'an. When Iblis refuses to bow to Adam, the reason he gives is a comparison: I am better than him, you made me from fire and him from clay. Before the refusal, a ranking. Then the Qur'an's advice from Luqman to his son, a father talking to a child: don't turn your cheek away from people in scorn, don't strut on the earth, and, in Pickthall's words, "Lo! Allah loveth not each braggart boaster." The cheek and the walk. Arrogance, in that verse, shows in the body. And last, the ordinary Tuesday. The cure for the first half is small. Someone corrects you, and they're right. You say: you're right. Said before the defense, before the but. A sound heart, from yesterday, has room in it for being wrong.
screen: `GOOD SANDALS ARE NOT THE PROBLEM.` · `REJECTING TRUTH, LOOKING DOWN.` · `IBLIS: I AM BETTER THAN HIM.` · then, large: `THE CHEEK AND THE WALK.`

segments.voice: The practice: accept one correction. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a time someone told you that you were wrong, and they had a point. A coworker, a child, a sibling, a stranger in traffic. Notice where the pushing away happened: the jaw, the tone, the quick reply. Now, quietly, give it the answer you didn't give then. They were right about that. Let it sit. If you pray, you can ask to be kept from kibr. If you don't, simply rest in the plain fact of it. The bell holds the time.
Kibr. Arrogance; in the hadith, rejecting the truth and looking down on people. Not good sandals. Today's word.

Your line: reject pride, not truth. Today, when someone corrects you and they have a point, let the first words out be: you're right. Tomorrow, a quieter disease: envy. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-two.

howItsDone: Muslim teachers count kibr, arrogance, among the diseases of the heart, using the hadith in Sahih Muslim that defines it as rejecting the truth and looking down on people; accepting correction is a common way of working against it.

match.prompt: the disease of arrogance — tap the pairs.

myth: in the hadith, liking good clothes and sandals is arrogance
the answer was that Allah is beautiful and loves beauty; kibr is rejecting truth and looking down on people.
the hadith's definition of arrogance includes rejecting the truth
kibr is rejecting the truth and looking down on people (Sahih Muslim).
the Qur'an's advice against strutting on the earth is given by Luqman to his son
a father to a child: don't turn your cheek in scorn, don't strut; Allah loveth not each braggart boaster.

fork.setup: you're in the gathering. a man asks: he likes his clothes and sandals to be good. is that the arrogance just warned about?
options: no: Allah is beautiful and loves beauty; kibr is rejecting truth and looking down on people.
only if they cost a lot.
fork.reveal: the sandals were never the problem. the hadith puts arrogance in two motions of the heart: pushing truth away and looking down on people.

original.note: Arabic: arrogance, pride; the word in the hadith in Sahih Muslim.

trapdoor: what you thought: arrogance means being rich, good-looking or well dressed.
what it means: kibr is rejecting the truth and looking down on people; Allah is beautiful and loves beauty.
what a scholar hears: the two-part definition in Sahih Muslim, read alongside Iblis's refusal and Luqman's advice to his son.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 91 (an atom's weight of arrogance; Allah is beautiful and loves beauty)

sources.quoted: Lo! Allah loveth not each braggart boaster.

notes: Sahih Muslim 91: confirm numbering and the paraphrase (atom's weight; the man's question about good clothes and sandals; 'Allah is beautiful and loves beauty'; kibr = rejecting truth and looking down on people).
Pickthall 31:18: confirm exact wording of 'Lo! Allah loveth not each braggart boaster.'
Iblis's reason (7:12) is paraphrased, not quoted.
Editor: cut the superlative 'the Qur'an's oldest picture of it' and the miscount 'three words' for 'you're right'.
